sources.title: Frustration and failure fuel Dyson's success
sources.notes: Tier 1/2 exclusive interview, 14 March 2013. States initial vacuum design had 5,127 changes; miniaturising cyclone took 5,127 tweaks between 1979 and 1984; rejected by British retailers; wife's income helped; Japan sales funded Malmesbury 1993; 'helped him on the way to becoming a billionaire'; inspiration from sawmill cyclone; first bagless was G-Force.

sources.title: James Dyson
sources.notes: Summarises ~5,127 prototypes over five years; G-Force 1983 Japan catalogue; no UK manufacturer/distributor would handle it because of replacement dust-bag market; dual cyclone patent EP0037674 (1980); founded own manufacturing; Malmesbury June 1993. Quotes Fast Company (May 2007): 'I made about 5,127 prototypes... There were 5,126 failures.'

sources.title: James Dyson on His Vacuum Failure and Success
sources.notes: Tier 2. Manufacturers had razor-and-blade bag/filter profits; refused license; 'if I wanted the technology out there, I'd have to do it myself'; Japan G-Force via Apex Limited; mid-80s Japan sales funded founding Dyson company 1993.

sources.title: Our Story
sources.notes: First-party foundation page. Affirms 5,127 prototypes headline and Hoover Junior / sawmill cyclone origin. Note: page conflates DC01 as 'first bagless' — prefer BBC/Wikipedia timeline (G-Force first). Used only as corroboration for prototype count and suction/bag frustration, not for DC01-as-first claim.

facts.claim: Dyson has said he made about 5,127 vacuum prototypes and that there were 5,126 failures before he got it right.
The bagless cyclone vacuum work ran roughly five years, with BBC placing the 5,127 tweaks between 1979 and 1984.
The frustration was a vacuum that lost suction / clogging bag performance; cyclone idea came from industrial sawdust separation.
Major manufacturers and UK distributors refused the bagless design because replacement dust bags were a profitable razor-and-blade business.
After licensing attempts failed, Dyson concluded he had to bring the technology to market himself (Japan G-Force sales, then his own manufacturing company).
The bagless machines succeeded commercially (Japan hit → UK factory 1993; Dual Cyclone became a major UK seller). BBC notes the redesign helped him toward becoming a billionaire.

unknown: Exact calendar date of each prototype count milestone (2,627 / 3,727) is memoir-sourced via secondary press — not used in spoken script.
Whether 'sold it himself' should mean Japan catalogue licensing vs later Malmesbury manufacturing — spoken uses the NY Mag 'do it myself' framing without inventing a single retail channel.
